DiffusionGemma, our experimental open model released under an Apache 2.0 license, explores text diffusion, an exceptionally fast approach to text generation.



Here’s how DiffusionGemma accelerates development:



+ Faster token output: By shifting the bottleneck from memory bandwidth to raw compute, the model generates up to 4x faster token output on dedicated GPUs

+ Accessible hardware footprint: Activates just 3.8B parameters during inference, fitting comfortably within 24GB-VRAM high-end consumer GPUs when quantized

+ Novel workflows: Parallel token generation enables self-correction, making it ideal for code infilling, in-line editing, and non-linear structures



DiffusionGemma prioritizes speed over raw quality and accelerates best on compute-bound hardware (like @NVIDIAAI GPUs). Standard @GoogleGemma 4 remains recommended for production quality and memory-bound devices.

There’s a ton of interest in custom model tuning as agents reach production and scale up. Here is how we made Databricks Knowledge Assistant 3x faster using our new Instructed Retriever model trained end-to-end to do parallel test-time compute. It’s rolling out to customers now!


Databricks AI Research (@DbrxMosaicAI)



Most agentic search systems get better by thinking longer: more tool calls, more reason-act loops, each step waiting on the last. Quality goes up, but so does latency.



Instructed-Retriever-1 takes a different route. Instead of scaling test-time compute sequentially, it scales it in parallel. One retrieval-specialized model fans the work out: it generates multiple query and filter formulations to widen recall, then reranks the merged evidence with a multi-pivot reranker to sharpen precision. Both stages run at once, so searching more broadly no longer means searching more slowly.



The result inside Knowledge Assistant: search time drops more than 3x and answer time 2x, with time to first token around two seconds, and no drop in quality (it matches Claude Sonnet 4.5 retrieval quality on KARLBench). For the people using it, that means far less waiting between question and answer, the freedom to ask more follow-ups, and more of the knowledge base actually surfaced. Rolling out to all customers now, with no reconfiguration.

We partnered with @trajectorylabs to post-train NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra for legal. Here’s what we found:



1) Open-weight models can reach frontier legal performance.



On our Legal Agent Benchmark (LAB), Nemotron 3 Ultra started at a 0% all-pass rate. After post-training, it reached 5.8%, placing it between Sonnet 4.6 at 4.2% and Opus 4.6 at 6.6%.



2) Post-training dramatically improves reliability.



Before training, many held-out tasks missed enough rubric dimensions to land around ~70% pass rates. After training, those tasks shifted toward ~95% pass rates.



3) Open-weight performance comes at much lower cost.



Post-trained Nemotron 3 Ultra reached a similar quality band to leading closed models while running at roughly 1/8th to 1/50th the per-token price of Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 4.6.



Most importantly: we post-trained this model on the @trajectorylabs platform less than 24 hours after Nemotron 3 Ultra launched, using the same harness, data, and recipe we used for Nemotron 3 Super.



More to come as we continue to experiment with open-weight legal agents.

We spent two decades securing users and machines. Now we have to secure what's in between: autonomous AI agents that authenticate, call tools, and make decisions at machine speed.



The problem? A prompt-injected agent doesn't look like an intruder. It looks like a trusted insider doing its job. Perimeter defenses were never built for that.



Zero Trust for the agentic era comes down to three ideas:



🔹 Never Trust, Always Verify: every agent request needs cryptographic auth, no matter its origin.



🔹 Least Agency: restrict not just access, but which tools an agent can use, how often, and where.



🔹 Assume Breach: contain the blast radius of any single compromised agent by design.

Ok. Let me make it extremely concrete.



Where did this giant sprawling datacenter come from?

It was printed out from the Internet.



Specifically, Zuck used the Internet to gather men, make money, organize materials, purchase territory, and shape it to advance Meta's goals.



The principal such goal is, ultimately, the replication of Meta itself. This datacenter makes money in the cloud, which enables Zuck to purchase more land, which he repeats all over the earth.



Think of it as viral growth, but in the physical world. Now extend that beyond Meta, towards any Internet tribe...such as your following.



After all, where was your following built? Was it built one handshake at a time? No, it was built on the Internet.



And where do you spend your time? Do you spend it convincing people in a small town? No, you probably spend it on the Internet.



And where do you make your money, use your money, find your information, talk to your ideologically aligned friends? Again and again, the Internet.



As Orwell said, to see what is in front of one's nose needs a constant struggle. The Internet is, right this moment, in front of your nose, as you're looking at your screen.



Yet despite being the single most important force in the world, the thing that billions personally engage with for hours per day, the driving force that essentially didn't even exist in daily life just a few decades ago, perhaps the most popular thing humans have ever created...the Internet is still somehow underestimated.

But Baran's initial idea remains important: even if the American state went down, the Internet's network would stay up. Concretely, what it means is that brilliant Americans designed a communications system that could survive even as everything else went down. So that we could restore America from cloud backup.



We might need to draw on that property. We might need to print out the Internet, to organize social networks in the physical world, to gather peers together online to start building the societies we believe in offline.

I want to share some thoughts about the impact of AI on org structure. 



This is based on early conversations with some of the top CHROs in Fortune 500 companies as well as other C-Suite leaders and startups. 



First: why do I think most enterprise org charts look the way they do? Maybe cleaner ownership lines (fiefdoms are fun), maybe easier to serve clients better (ex: the API team at OpenAI shouldn't be separate from the ChatGPT team because the same clients are buying both and don't want to deal with two separate teams), maybe just redundancies and catching errors. 



Layers of people in orgs end up acting like an org sieve or one of those coin sorters. Issues come up, and because multiple people or departments have to review it, many of them are caught ahead of time. 



The structure helps to absorb human mistakes. 



It's a liability support system.



AI-First companies (which tend to be companies trying to reduce friction and create flatter orgs) are pulling out those layers on purpose. 



And as a result, ownership (one person running hundreds or thousands of agents) is getting more concentrated.



If ownership gets MORE concentrated because of layer removal, then that actually RAISES the trust you need in your people, your team, your company. 



When one marketer or finance leader owns an entire outcome, you as the leader have to trust their taste, their risk tolerance, their judgement, their level of "done", etc. a whole lot more because there is no one downstream to fix it. 



And so what happens as a result? The hiring math changes. You're less likely to bring in outsiders into your org (so internal referrals and employees with strong networks become even more important). The CEO is more likely to get back in the weeds and have more conversations with owners. You're more likely to have layers of AI as filters and judges, verifying whether work has been completed to a certain quality level. And I'd argue B players have a harder time hiding and are less likely to be kept. 



AI-first orgs are higher stakes per seat, and I think it has actual implications for hiring, growing, staffing, collaborating, referring, firing, and scaling. 



Change management in enterprises takes years, so we'll see this play out slowly over the next 18 months.

Something I've been confused about for years has snapped into focus. Updating on information is a specific mental move that improves with practice. I've never really seen anyone (besides maybe Eliezer in the sequences? Don't remember) try to describe it. I'm so acclimated to it that it did not occur to me that it was a missing step. It isn't always the same but here are some moves it often calls on. I want to emphasize that these sound effortful when you haven't already done them thousands of times, just like any other skill, but they are actually pretty rapid in real time. 



Noticing that there is an opportunity to update. Pausing. curiosity about the value of the update. Imagining the ways things might go if you do make the update. Imagining ways they might go if you do not make the update. A feeling of the one time costs and the ongoing maintenance costs of the update. A sense of which people will be affected besides me and what it might mean to them. Imagining concretely the different action taken if the update is made and how that feels. Open space for concerns/objections to the update. Commitment to provisionally trying something.



Again these don't always all occur, thought is messier than description. I also don't always do this even when I should. It seems to me like availability of these moves (and others like them that I'm forgetting) allow more freeform empiricism, trying on beliefs, calibration, dissolving stuck priors, and believing in things that seem worth believing. Also help a lot in primary relationship since you both want to update on what your partner wants and you want those to be changeable along with their dynamism.

Biggest of all is that I’ve been working a lot on AI agent harnesses, skills, tools, and apps that make it all make sense to the human in the driver seat.



My POV on agents and skills has changed a lot. I’m now a fan (in most cases).



At the same time, I’ve evolved into a software engineer.



I still can barely write a lick of code by hand, but that doesn’t matter. And I say this not to brag, but to inspire (I hope). I’d say at this point I’m a 10x engineer. I have totally outpaced most of the traditional software engineers I interact with, even though they have access to the same tools.



By the end of the year, I expect to be a 100x engineer.



When you can’t look at the code and know whether it’s good, you have no choice but to build systems around it. That’s something I hope to teach at some point, but I’m still knee-deep in it right now.



For coding harnesses, I use Codex as my main driver (via 2 x $200/month ChatGPT subscriptions) with Claude for a bunch of more specialized work (1 x $200/month).



My setup evolves constantly, so it feels like there’s never a good moment to stop and say, “This is the way to do it,” but I am trying to at least capture a snapshot for you.



Not just for coding.



For *everything*.



Almost anything I used to use Make or N8N for... or GPTs, prompts, all that stuff, it's now just *here* as skills and workflows and SOPs and Obsidian vaults (folders full of markdown text files) that connect to all of it.



Real soon I hope to publish what I’m calling my Personal OS.



I’m barely in the actual ChatGPT or Claude web chat anymore. I’m in this.



Personal OS will be a snapshot of what I use daily. I'm trying to get it to set itself up for you depending on your needs and what you have already. It'll come with the business-focused skills and things and I think the coding stuff will be an optional upgrade.



I’ve been working for weeks to turn this in this template that sets itself up, and a short 1-hour course about these agent harness things and how to use them to be a 10x or 100x of whatever you want to be.



People have been asking for it, so I’m delivering.



Here’s what my typical day looks like:



After getting the kiddos off to school and the dog walked, I’m running Codex and Claude apps across two monitors, along with some Obsidian vaults and a few web browsers.



I’ll be managing 3-5 workstreams at a time, with agents performing research, coding up new features, exploring ideas, managing my task list, checking my email, investigating bugs, building a little hobby app on the side… whatever I think they can do for me.



Maybe 30% of the messages I send invoke one or more skills. This is where prompt engineering has evolved to, although a skill is often much more than a prompt.



The two skills I use the most are called “Now what? Figure out a plan” and “Fresh eyes”. You can probably guess a little about what they do.



So anything I do often becomes a skill, and it’s something I work with the agent to improve over time. Any time I use the skill and I don’t like how it went, I might update it. 95% of the time I tell the AI to update its own skill based on what I want. A by-hand pass over a skill often reveals ways to improve it, in minor ways, but usually it’s not necessary unless it’s a core file like your root AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md files.



Not everything can be AI-driven, obviously, so I'm regularly stopping, reviewing, planning, figuring stuff out. That can be the hardest transition, like going 100 mph on the freeway and having to suddenly get out of the car and start walking every once and a while.



But it can be good to slow down and go outside sometimes, right?



SO.



Will I start creating content again regularly?



It’s hard to say definitively. I love building and I’m hoping to continue that. But I’ve discovered so much, it feels wasteful not to share. So I’m trying to get back into it.



This is a crazy moment in history.

​

What's possible today wasn't possible 6 months ago.

​

I’m doing everything I can to capture it. To play the role I want to play in it as best I can.



But boy-oh-boy, even with 3 mega subscriptions and 5 agents running all day, I never can seem to get all the work done. But that’s maybe because I’m aiming for 10-100x bigger goals than I ever have before.



Hope you’re well.

Years ago someone asked me what comes after the AI-first enterprise. I said the autonomous enterprise.



The core of it is a flywheel: four parts (well, five including feedback) that feed each other, and every loop makes the next one smarter:



→ Goals - what is the company prioritizing, what does each team own, what does good look like

→ Context - everything that's happened before, plus current day goings-on, plus your resources (budget, tokens, people)

→ Action - where work actually gets done, SOPs and skills so AI can execute against Gmail, Calendar, Salesforce, other data, tradeoff analysis against goals and context, simulations

→ Decisions - what actions were taken, the memory layer, where the system reflects on what worked and feeds it back in

→ Feedback (duh)



You'll hear it called closed loops. Satya Nadella called it hill climbing to a small room a few weeks. But I worked at Amazon for four years, so it's going to be a flywheel in my head until I die.



The hard part of all of this is the plumbing (ex: connecting AI into your tools safely, pulling the judgment out of your company, extracting and reviewing your processes, codifying your qualities and value, governance and documentation to be able to interpret and review what is happening) - and managing it so the system acts the way you actually want. Then monitoring the whole thing constantly, with humans and with AI.



And trust me when I say that single exec workshop I'm doing right now is on building a self-learning org and carving out this flywheel.
And it's been deeply gratifying to watch this come together—every layer, from the hardware up, built and owned by us. 😇
